Most people don't quit sports because they stopped loving the game. They quit because matching four calendars, finding a court and working around a sore knee takes too much group chat.
So for this hackathon, I built Serve. Not an AI coach. A club where your agent sorts things out with your friends' agents, and only asks you for one yes.

Here's a live run of my week. Monday, I tell it my right knee is sore. Serve never gives medical advice. Muse Glimmer files it on my body, and turns it into a rule for my week: doubles first, and one game fewer.

Autopilot takes over. Muse Glimmer, on my own RTX 3090, calls one tool at a time. Then it negotiates with three friends' agents at once, over A2A. Agents only mark which times work; code picks from the overlap. Nothing is booked until I say yes.
Any ball sport works. Prompt Guard 2 screens the Google reviews, then Glimmer judges four courts at once. A reason that doesn't quote its source is dropped by code.

Thursday, game done. I upload a phone clip. DETR finds the players, Sapiens2 finds the fastest swing, and SAM 2.1 cuts me out. With MapAnything, time stops and the camera turns around the smash. {+2} Glimmer writes the caption, and it's one tap to Instagram.
After the game, Glimmer reads a photo of the scoreboard, code checks the score against the rules, and my club ranking moves.

Logging 2,755 calls, I found that 84% of Glimmer's tokens are reasoning. Even with thinking off, it reasoned in a hidden channel, and came back empty. So every call leaves room to think. And a local Llama 3.2 1B, distilled from Glimmer, now answers 54 to 67% of members' decisions in my simulated club, with no rule broken.
Every agent follows Meta's Agents Rule of Two. And a disclosure budget cuts how much of your week a snooping agent can pin down, from 97.6% to 32.4%.
And the club evolves itself. Members' ideas are grouped with DRAMA, voted on, built by a coding agent behind nine gates, and rolled back on their own if feedback drops.
That's Serve. Play more, manage less.
